Introduction to JupyterLab¶

What is Jupyter?¶

  • Jupyter grew out of another project called interactive python, or ipython
  • The name jupyter is a portmanteau of julia, python, and R
  • JupyterLab is a web-based development environment including notebooks, editors, terminals, etc.

Why use Jupyter?¶

  • to make pretty pages like this one
  • interactive code development
  • to make interactive scripts for other people to use
  • to record your workflow (ie, as a lab book)

Exercise 1: starting a session¶

  • Go to https://ondemand.talapas.uoregon.edu/
  • Login
  • Choose Clusters -> Shell access
  • Before you go, run these commands:
    • echo $PATH | grep -o : | wc -l # show how many paths are in your $PATH
    • env | wc -l # show how many variables are defined in your environment
  • Go to interactive apps and start a jupyter lab session
    • Default options are fine
    • Leave custom conda environment unchecked
[emwin@login2 ~]$ echo $PATH | grep -o : | wc -l 8 [emwin@login2 ~]$ env | wc -l 75

The Jupyter Lab Interface¶

Left sidebar: shows the file browser, running kernels, etc.¶

  • File browser: You can only navigate to folders beneath your own home folder. You can upload and download files to your local computer here.
  • Running kernels: Shows open tabs and running kernels.
    • Open tabs: self explanatory
    • Kernels: running kernels and the notebooks using them. Notebooks can share a kernel but things can get weird.
    • Language servers: You will probably never use this, the functionality is disabled by default
    • Terminals: Any open terminals (they'll also show under tabs)
    • Workspaces: Newer versions of Jupyter Lab will also show workspaces here
  • Table of contents: shows markdown headers
  • Extension manager: jupyter lab add-ons
  • Software modules: shows modules that have been loaded, or that can be loaded. LOADING MODULES HERE IS NOT RECOMMENDED.

Right sidebar: property inspector and debugger¶

  • Property inspector
    • Common tools: you can write protect individual cells and add tags
    • Advanced tools: beyond the scope of this workshop
  • Debugger: also beyond the scope of this workshop

Menu bar¶

  • File
  • Edit
  • View
  • Run
  • Kernel
  • Tabs
  • Settings
  • Help

Main work area¶

Where your tabs for your notebooks, terminals, launchers, editor, etc are.

Exercise 2: The terminal¶

  • Click the blue "+" button that says "New Launcher" when you hover over it, or choose the Launcher tab if it's already open

  • Create a terminal

  • Are you on a login node?

  • Try these commands:

ls /cephfs # This is the remote storage location for research groups
python3 --version
python --version
echo $PATH | grep -o : | wc -l
env | wc -l

module purge
echo $PATH | grep -o : | wc -l
env | wc -l
[emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ hostname n0398.talapas.uoregon.edu [emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ ls /cephfs # This is the remote storage location for research groups ls: cannot access '/cephfs': No such file or directory [emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ python3 --version Python 3.15.2 [emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ python --version Python 3.15.2 [emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ echo $PATH | grep -o : | wc -l 21 [emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ env | wc -l 368 [emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ module list Currently Loaded Modules: 1) latex/20250228 2) miniconda3/20260319 [emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ module purge Warning: Conda environment still active. Run 'conda deactivate' before unloading. [emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ echo $PATH | grep -o : | wc -l 16 [emwin@n0398 jupyter-f26]$ env | wc -l 348
  • Now try ssh login.talapas.uoregon.edu and repeat the first six commands. When you're done, don't forget to exit.
[emwin@login2 ~]$ ls /cephfs # This is the remote storage location for research groups ... [emwin@login2 ~]$ python3 --version Python 3.6.8 [emwin@login2 ~]$ python --version -bash: python: command not found [emwin@login2 ~]$ module list No modules loaded [emwin@login2 ~]$ module purge [emwin@login2 ~]$ echo $PATH | grep -o : | wc -l 8

Takeaways from exercise 2¶

  • You can only browse the /cephfs volume (large scale research storage) from a login node
  • You can get to a login node using ssh
  • The commands you run may give different results depending on your current environment
  • module purge does not get you back to the same environment you would have on a login node, or in a talapas desktop session

Conda environments and JupyterLab¶

  • The default jupyter lab OnDemand app is running in a conda environment that you can't modify
  • If you build your own conda environment that includes Jupyter, you can:
    • use a more recent Jupyter version
    • use a more recent python version
    • add support for more kernels, such as R
    • create custom kernels
    • add python packages you need

jupyter.yml example file¶

name: myjupyter
channels:
  - conda-forge
dependencies:
  - numpy
  - pandas
  - seaborn
  - jupyter
  - r-base
  - r-essentials
  - r-irkernel
  - nodejs
  - ipywidgets
  - pip
  - pip:
    - git+https://github.com/conery/nbscan.git

Exercise 3: Creating and saving notebooks¶

  • Click the blue "+" button that says "New Launcher" when you hover over it
  • Create a new notebook using the ipykernel
  • Choose File->Save Notebook As and give the notebook a name
  • Look at the tabs with the notebook names. If there's a solid circle next to the name, it indicates unsaved changes. After it autosaves it changes to ×
  • Hovering over the tab will show you the name, path, last save, and last checkpoint
  • To make a checkpoint: use the save icon or hit Ctrl-S.
  • You can revert to the last checkpoint, but not further back than that -- there is only one checkpoint at a time.
  • Look at Open Tabs and Running Kernels. If you close a notebook, does the kernel stop?

Interactive python¶

Everything after this will focus on notebooks using the interactive python kernel ipykernel. Other kernels (eg R) will not have all of these features!

Cells¶

Notebooks consist of cells. There are three types:

  • Markdown: like this one. They look nice.
  • Raw: good for comments
  • Code: for actually doing things
This is a raw cell.

After you type something into a cell, hit the "play" button or shift-enter to run it.

Code cells run any code within the cell, and show stdout and stderr beneath the cell. If the code cell returns a value, it will be shown as an output cell.

In [1]:
# this is a code cell. It returns a value
'Hello ' + 'World'
Out[1]:
'Hello World'
In [2]:
# this code cell prints to std out
print('Hello World')

Hello World
In [3]:
# this code cell has an error
pirnt('Hello World')

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
NameError                                 Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[3], line 2
      1 # this code cell has an error
----> 2 pirnt('Hello World')

NameError: name 'pirnt' is not defined

We can edit and rerun cells, copy them, drag them around, etc. Be careful about doing too much of that if you are using the notebook as a lab book.

Variables and Functions¶

Variables and functions defined in a cell are accessible anywhere in the rest of the notebook.

In [4]:
hw = 'Hello ' + 'World'
print(hw)

Hello World
In [5]:
hw
Out[5]:
'Hello World'
In [6]:
def hello(input):
    print('Hello ' + input)
In [7]:
hello('World')

Hello World
In [8]:
def goodbye(input):
    return 'Goodbye ' + input
In [9]:
goodbye('World')
Out[9]:
'Goodbye World'
In [10]:
gw = goodbye('World')
In [11]:
gw
Out[11]:
'Goodbye World'
You can suppress the returned value by adding a semicolon at the end -- if you're a matlab user this will be familiar
In [12]:
goodbye('World');
In & Out¶

See those numbers next to some output cells? There are two special containers called "In" and "Out". All code cells go into the "In" container. All output cells go into the "Out" container. Those containers are saved during the current session, no matter how many times you re-execute a code cell.

In [13]:
In
Out[13]:
['',
 "# this is a code cell. It returns a value\n'Hello ' + 'World'",
 "# this code cell prints to std out\nprint('Hello World')",
 "# this code cell has an error\npirnt('Hello World')",
 "hw = 'Hello ' + 'World'\nprint(hw)",
 'hw',
 "def hello(input):\n    print('Hello ' + input)",
 "hello('World')",
 "def goodbye(input):\n    return 'Goodbye ' + input",
 "goodbye('World')",
 "gw = goodbye('World')",
 'gw',
 "goodbye('World');",
 'In']
In [14]:
Out
Out[14]:
{1: 'Hello World',
 5: 'Hello World',
 9: 'Goodbye World',
 11: 'Goodbye World',
 13: ['',
  "# this is a code cell. It returns a value\n'Hello ' + 'World'",
  "# this code cell prints to std out\nprint('Hello World')",
  "# this code cell has an error\npirnt('Hello World')",
  "hw = 'Hello ' + 'World'\nprint(hw)",
  'hw',
  "def hello(input):\n    print('Hello ' + input)",
  "hello('World')",
  "def goodbye(input):\n    return 'Goodbye ' + input",
  "goodbye('World')",
  "gw = goodbye('World')",
  'gw',
  "goodbye('World');",
  'In',
  'Out']}

'In' is a python list and 'Out' is a python dict. Notice what's not in Out: anything written to stdout or stderr. This will matter when we introduce logging.

In [15]:
In[1]
Out[15]:
"# this is a code cell. It returns a value\n'Hello ' + 'World'"
In [16]:
Out[1]
Out[16]:
'Hello World'
There's a shortcut to get the last output: _
In [17]:
_
Out[17]:
'Hello World'

Logging¶

The ipykernel has a built-in logging command which can let us use jupyter as an electronic lab book.

In [21]:
%logstart?

Docstring:
Start logging anywhere in a session.

%logstart [-o|-r|-t|-q] [log_name [log_mode]]

If no name is given, it defaults to a file named 'ipython_log.py' in your
current directory, in 'rotate' mode (see below).

'%logstart name' saves to file 'name' in 'backup' mode.  It saves your
history up to that point and then continues logging.

%logstart takes a second optional parameter: logging mode. This can be one
of (note that the modes are given unquoted):

append
    Keep logging at the end of any existing file.

backup
    Rename any existing file to name~ and start name.

global
    Append to  a single logfile in your home directory.

over
    Overwrite any existing log.

rotate
    Create rotating logs: name.1~, name.2~, etc.

Options:

  -o
    log also IPython's output. In this mode, all commands which
    generate an Out[NN] prompt are recorded to the logfile, right after
    their corresponding input line. The output lines are always
    prepended with a '#[Out]# ' marker, so that the log remains valid
    Python code.

  Since this marker is always the same, filtering only the output from
  a log is very easy, using for example a simple awk call::

    awk -F'#\[Out\]# ' '{if($2) {print $2}}' ipython_log.py

  -r
    log 'raw' input.  Normally, IPython's logs contain the processed
    input, so that user lines are logged in their final form, converted
    into valid Python.  For example, %Exit is logged as
    _ip.run_line_magic("Exit").  If the -r flag is given, all input is logged
    exactly as typed, with no transformations applied.

  -t
    put timestamps before each input line logged (these are put in
    comments).

  -q
    suppress output of logstate message when logging is invoked
File:      ~/.conda/envs/pandas-f26/lib/python3.15/site-packages/IPython/core/magics/logging.py
